thread.title: A Pension Bought Apple Stock at the Wrong Time - Barron's

title: A Pension Bought Apple Stock at the Wrong Time - Barron's
text:
A Pension Fund Bought Apple Stock at the Wrong Time By Jan. 9, 2019 7:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Yu Kato Text size
The pension fund of Dutch chemicals company DSM, bulked up on Apple stock (ticker: AAPL) at an unfortunate time.
PDN, as the pension fund formally called Stichting Pensioenfonds DSM Nederland is known, bought 8,700 more shares of the iPhone maker in the fourth quarter. That raised its stake to 62,600 shares at the end of 2018, according to a form PDN filed to the Securities and Exchange Commission . Apple was wrapping up its worst calendar year in terms of stock performance since the financial crisis , so perhaps the pension thought the shares were cheap. Unfortunately, Apple made an uncharacteristic earnings warning just last week, and the stock is now down 4.5% so far this year through Tuesday’s close while the wider market has been rallying .
The purchase is a glaring misstep by a pension that has been quite successful by some measures. As of the end of November, PDN’s funding level was 107.9% , meaning the pension could more than meet its payout requirements. The Dutch government requires that pensions have funding levels of at least 105% . Many American counterparts would struggle to meet that. The Wall Street Journal reported in October that defined-benefit pension plans of S&P 500 companies were only 91% funded at the end of September, based on data from Goldman Sachs Asset Management.
PDN has its own measures of achievement, and a funding level of 107.9% misses its internal target of 110% for increasing pension payouts. “Each year, PDN endeavors to raise the pensions of pensioners and the accrued pensions of former members,” the pension wrote in its 2017 annual report , the latest such update. PDN didn’t equivocate when it noted that “as things look now the chances of increasing the pensions in any of the coming years are remote.”
PDN didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The pension certainly can’t fault Apple’s stock drop as having a material effect on its outlook. In fact, U.S. assets are only a small part of the pension’s portfolio. At the end of the third quarter, PDN had 7 billion euros in assets , while its investment in U.S.-traded securities stood at a mere $505.4 million as of Dec. 31 .
In any case, PDN is making sizeable bets in American blue chips. It initiated positions in Verizon Communications stock (VZ), McDonald’s stock (MCD), and CVS Health stock (CVS) in the fourth quarter. The pension also exited an investment in Eli Lilly stock (LLY).
The pension bought 96,000 shares of telecom giant Verizon in the fourth quarter. We’ve noted that Verizon topped peers in 2018 , and its wireless-subscriber growth is topping expectations , suggesting that the good times may continue to roll for this Dow Jones Industrial Average component.
McDonald’s is another Dow stock that rose in 2018 ; it gained nearly 6%, excluding dividend payments, but that handily beats the nearly 6% drop in the index. Morgan Stanley analyst John Glass sees another standout year in 2019 . PDN bought 22,500 shares of the burger chain in the fourth quarter.
The pension also bought CVS stock in the quarter, ending the year with 15,415 shares of the drugstore chain and pharmacy benefits manager. Barron’s recently noted that CVS has become a rather cheap stock after a 7% drop in 2018. CVS closed the acquisition of Aetna in November, but received a credit-rating downgrade in return .
Eli Lilly stock had a boffo 2018, soaring nearly 41%, and the company also issued upbeat guidance in December . The pharma giant is one stock that PDN had traded in and out of during the year, records show. At the end of March , the pension owned 49,600 Lilly shares. It owned none three months later , only to show an investment of 40,000 Lilly shares by the end of September . When 2018 ended, PDN didn’t own any Eli Lilly stock .
Write to Ed Lin at and follow @BarronsEdLin .
